extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent attorneys, and judges handling patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for what evidence is required and admissible in patent causes, and the substantive standards for the sufficiency/enablement of a patent specification, especially in injunction and infringement contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of affidavits on motions to grant or dissolve injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether affidavits can be read on a motion to grant or to dissolve an injunction (including after an answer has been filed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The admission of affidavits in injunction motions is governed by the court's sound discretion, particularly where 'irreparable mischief' is alleged. By analogy to cases of waste and partnership, affidavits may be allowed at certain stages even against an answer; there has been conflict in decisions, but established practice permits affidavits to be read both by plaintiff and defendant to support or repel an injunction. See discussion of authority (e.g., Poor v. Carleton) and Lord Langdale's dictum that a defendant may displace affidavits by his answer — interpreted to mean the answer may control a prima facie case but does not necessarily automatically displace affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court discretion in injunctions for irreparable mischief
rubrics_metrics.description: The granting or dissolving of injunctions in cases of irreparable harm rests in the sound discretion of the court whether applied for before or after answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court must balance the possibility of irreparable injury (e.g., that harm would occur before the plaintiff could establish rights at law) against the defendant's right to have denials (such as denial of novelty) tried at law. The options are (a) assume the answer's denial true (barring injunctions in many cases), (b) always grant injunctions despite denials, or (c) examine the evidence on both sides sufficiently to determine the probability of the plaintiff's success and grant or withhold the injunction accordingly (the latter course recommended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence in patent causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence in patent litigation is usefully divided into evidence of title and evidence of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of title relates to the letters-patent, the plaintiff's interest, the novelty and utility of the invention, and the sufficiency of the specification. Evidence of infringement relates to the identity of what the defendant made, used, or practiced with the invention claimed by the patentee. Different proof rules and witnesses may apply to each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of letters-patent as competent evidence of grant
rubrics_metrics.description: A copy of the patent under the patent office seal and the commissioner's signature is competent evidence that a patent has been granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Statute of 1836 a certified copy is sufficient evidence the government granted the patent for the invention described. If the patent in evidence refers to a description in a former patent, the former patent must be produced and read to show what the invention is where the present patent does not make the invention entirely clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie presumption of validity and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The letters-patent, once proved, are prima facie evidence that the patentee was the first inventor; the burden of proof shifts to the party objecting to show the grant was improperly obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption rests on the patentee's statutory oath that he is the first and true inventor and on the presumption that public officers performed their duties properly. An objector must show by evidence that the patent was granted improperly; courts will not reexamine the sufficiency of proofs before the issuing officer absent contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must offer some evidence that the invention is capable of some use beneficial to society (utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of utility is immaterial so long as some useful purpose exists. Utility is ordinarily proved by testimony from persons conversant with the subject (experts) saying whether the invention can be used or is an improvement, but may also be shown by evidence such as large public orders or licenses taken for the exercise of the right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of the specification (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must show the specification is 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, as to enable any person, skilled in the art or science to which it appertains, to make, construct, compound, or use' the thing patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the specification is sufficient may sometimes be apparent on its face; where complicated or technical, the plaintiff should give evidence (often slight evidence at opening) that skilled persons can apply the specification. If sufficiency is disputed, the plaintiff must introduce evidence to sustain it. The amount of evidence in opening versus later depends on trial circumstances, but slight initial proof is generally enough to put the defendant to the task of falsifying the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper witnesses: persons 'skilled in the art or science'
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate witnesses to determine sufficiency are those 'skilled in the art or science' — generally practical workmen of ordinary skill in the particular branch of industry to which the patent relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute's phrase can include both practical artisans and higher scientific persons, but the law adopts practical skilled workmen as the general standard because specifications are addressed to those who will apply them in practice. Where the invention falls within a trade practiced by particular mechanics, operators, manufacturers, or other workmen, their capacity to carry out the specification without invention or addition is the test. Higher theoretical witnesses may be relevant where the subject matter requires it, but the primary standard is the competent practical workman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-specific application of the sufficiency test
rubrics_metrics.description: How the sufficiency/enablement standard is applied depends on the type of invention: machines, compositions of matter, or processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for a pump or mechanical improvement, ask whether an ordinary pump-maker could construct it from the specification; for a chemical composition, whether a practical chemist of ordinary skill could make the compound by following directions; for a process applying a physical principle in manufacture, whether a competent workman following directions would produce the intended effect. The standard adapts to the nature of the art involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose best mode and particulars known to patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee acquainted with any particular mode by which the invention may be most conveniently carried into effect ought to state it in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose known helpful details (e.g., use of tallow in a process) can render the specification bad. The specification must not merely suggest a method that sets the public to experimenting or require trials; it must plainly set forth the invention and how to carry it into effect so as to save others the trouble and expense of experiments. Statements that leave essential parameters to 'be learned by experience' risk invalidity unless such judgment is within ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of drawings and necessity for directions/dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are illustrative of the invention and not necessarily limiting; nevertheless, the specification must provide directions (and where necessary dimensions or instructions) sufficient to enable construction without experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A drawing alone, without directions or dimensions when those are necessary, is insufficient if the missing information can only be ascertained by subsequent experiment. The drawing should be treated as illustrative; the specification must contain either specific instructions or satisfy that a workman of ordinary skill could construct the device (e.g., find eccentric centre or rod lengths) without resort to experiments. If the figure were taken as limiting, proof of infringement would require identical angles/dimensions, which is not the intended rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple inventions in one patent must each be supported
rubrics_metrics.description: If a single patent attempts to claim two or more inventions, each invention must be separately useful and sufficiently described in the specification to support it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee who 'runs the hazard of putting two inventions into one patent' cannot hold the patent unless each invention can be supported as a separate patent — each must be useful and described so people clearly know what the invention is and how to carry it into effect. Example: a patent claiming both a steam-engine and separate machinery for propelling vessels must sufficiently specify each invention.
